title: React Components
summary: Introduces React function components: a function with a PascalCase name that returns JSX, used as a custom tag. Shows splitting a Heading and a List out of one file into separate .jsx modules with default export and import, then the App component and components folder layout.

concepts.heading: Why components
points: Long single files are hard to read; components split a big page into small, focused pieces.
A component can be reused wherever the same markup is needed, e.g. two List components without rewriting the ul and li tags.
Real components (heading with wrapper div, nav bar, styles) are much larger than the tiny examples used here.

concepts.heading: Writing a function component
points:
A component is a JavaScript function that returns JSX: function Heading() { return

My Favourite Foods

; }.
The name must be PascalCase (every word capitalised). React uses the capital first letter to tell a custom component from a built-in HTML tag; lowercase names are treated as DOM elements.
Use it like a tag: <Heading />. When React reaches that tag it calls the function and puts the returned elements where the tag was.

Components without children should use a self-closing tag with a space before the slash (<Heading />). This follows the Airbnb React/JSX style guide, a commonly cited convention reference; a linter may auto-fix it. The compiler does not care, it is for readability.
Do not add parentheses in the export (export default Heading), since that would call the function immediately instead of handing it over.

concepts.heading: One component per file (ES6 modules)
points: Put each component in its own file named after it with the .jsx extension (Heading.jsx). Convention: the entry file (index.js / main.jsx) stays plain JS, components use .jsx.

Older setups required import React from "react" at the top of every component file so JSX could be compiled; the lecture does this each time. (Extra) With the modern JSX transform used by Vite and React 17+, this import is no longer needed, which is why the reference repo omits it.
At the bottom of the component file: export default Heading;. In the file that uses it: import Heading from "./Heading"; (relative path starting with ./).
File extensions are optional in the import path in the sandbox; the bundler resolves Heading to Heading.jsx.
Being the default export means the importer can pick any local name, but keeping it the same as the component is standard. (Extra)

concepts.heading: The App component and project structure
points: Typical apps keep the entry file nearly empty: it only renders <App /> into the root element.
App.jsx defines the top of the component tree, returning a div containing <Heading /> and <List />, and is exported as default.
A component must return one root element (here a div, or a fragment <>...</>).

As the number of components grows, put them in a components folder (src/components) and update relative import paths accordingly, e.g. ./components/App. Larger apps further group by feature such as login or register screens.

task.name: Extract a List component
task.starting_point: Sandbox where Heading has been extracted already, and the h1 plus ul still sit in the entry file.
task.goal: Create a List component in its own file and use it in place of the inline ul.
steps: Create List.jsx inside src (use the new-file button, not new-folder).
Add the React import if the setup requires it, then define function List() returning the ul with its three li items.
Add export default List at the bottom.
In the entry/App file delete the ul markup, write <List /> as a self-closing tag, and import List from "./List".
Optionally restructure so the entry file only renders <App />, with App.jsx holding Heading and List inside a div, and move everything into a components folder, fixing the import paths.
task.expected_result: The page looks identical to before (heading and list), but the markup lives in three small files.

pitfalls: A lowercase component name (heading) is treated as an HTML tag and renders nothing useful.
Writing export default Heading() calls the function instead of exporting it.
Forgetting to import a component gives a 'List is not defined' error.
Moving files into a folder breaks relative import paths until they are updated.
The new-folder and new-file buttons in the sandbox sit side by side; choose the correct one.
